## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
No trials yet, and the starting architecture scores 0 on both seeds. The default budget allows only 131,072 steps, which is 32 PPO updates of 4,096 samples. That is very few for exact builds of 6–16 bricks, so the recipe may be the main bottleneck rather than the architecture. A network smaller than the starting one gets no extra samples (r below 1 counts as 1), so I keep the cost near r≈1 and spend the room on structure. The candidates form a small factorial design. C1 keeps the starting architecture and changes only the recipe: 2 PPO epochs (about 1.9x more samples), gamma 0.98, lambda 0.95 and lower entropy. C2 uses the same recipe with a new network: a per-layer column encoder shared across heights, normalised residual 3x3 blocks, a footprint-pooling spatial head, and separate DONE and value MLPs. C3 is the same network with 1 epoch and 512 envs × 8 steps. All code reads X, Y, Z, the channel count and the footprints from spec.

### Round 2
All four runs, the start and r1c1 to r1c3, score 0 on dev and 0 on training success in the last 10% of training. These include a recipe-only change (2 epochs, gamma 0.98), a layer-encoder ResNet, and the same ResNet with 1 epoch and about 426k steps. So neither more samples nor a better recipe alone gives any success. The likely bottleneck is the network's form. To score a placement, the net must find the landing layer (the highest build cell under the footprint) and then check that every footprint cell is missing at that same layer. 2D nets that put layers in channels must learn this cross-cell, layer-indexed AND from scratch. This round tests a voxel network. It computes learned per-(layer, cell) features with z-convs, cummax up and down the column after a learned layer, and a 3x3 conv per layer. Footprint max/min/avg pooling is applied within each layer and the per-layer scores are combined with logsumexp over z. The training cost stays near the start's (r≈1.1). Three candidates: the voxel net with the 2-epoch recipe, the same net with 1 epoch, and a wider net with 1 epoch.

### Round 3
All 6 trials (12 seeds) got exactly 0 training success and 0 dev success. These covered 2D ResNets, a voxel head with support cummax, 1 vs 2 PPO epochs, 205k–426k steps, and ent_coef 0.003 vs 0.01. Even a sloppy but correctly wired agent should exactly build some 6-brick designs with 1x1 bricks, so zero everywhere suggests something structural, not a tuning problem. My suspicion: the world's action index layout does not match the observation's spatial layout. It could be transposed (y↔x), cell-major (cell×type instead of type×cell), or use a different anchor. Every candidate so far scores placements with a translation-equivariant conv head that flattens as [type, y, x]. If the layout differs, each logit reads features from the wrong cell, and local receptive fields cannot fix that. This round tests the layout hypothesis three ways, keeping the r1c1 recipe so the head is the only change.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored exactly 0 on dev and 0 on training success. That held across trunks (start, layer-encoder ResNet, voxel), heads (pooled conv, FC, MLP, multi-layout) and recipes (1 or 2 epochs, entropy 0.003 or 0.01). Since even training success is 0, the shared bottleneck is probably not the trunk. It is more likely the DONE action. Every design used a flat softmax over 256 placements plus DONE, with a tiny-initialised DONE output. That makes P(DONE) about 0.4% per step, so a completed build is almost never followed by DONE. Without DONE, the +1 exact-build bonus is never seen, and greedy evaluation never stops. In this last round every candidate splits the policy into two learned parts: a gate that chooses DONE or place (sigmoid, zero-initialised, about 0.5 at start), then a softmax over placements. The main risk is the agent learning to call DONE at once. The default entropy of 0.01 is meant to counter that.
